---
title: "Plausibility checks"
description: "How OPDI leaves out the flight milestones that the aircraft's own track contradicts, such as an off-block time while the aircraft is flying, and how often a removed time was one that the airport confirms."
---

## What it is

An **event**, or milestone, says that something happened to a flight at a
given time: the aircraft left its stand, took off, crossed a flight level.
Each event is found by a detector, a set of rules applied to the position
reports of one **track** (the reports that OPDI treats as one flight; see
[Track identity](track-identity.qmd)). A detector can be wrong. It can, for
example, place an in-block time (`AIBT`, the moment the aircraft stops at its
stand) while the aircraft is still several thousand feet above the airport.

The position reports of the same track say what the aircraft was really doing
at that time: how high it was above the airport, how fast it moved over the
ground, and whether its transponder reported it as on the ground. Where these
facts clearly contradict an event, the event cannot be true. The
**plausibility checks** find such events and leave them out of the published
data.

The checks apply to all event families. They run in step 04 of the
[processing steps](pipeline.qmd#events-and-measurements), after every event
has been detected and before anything is written. A removed event:

- does not appear in the flight events file, and its measurements go with it;
- is not used for the columns of the flight list that repeat a milestone
  (`aobt`, `aibt`, `atot`, `aldt` and the stand and runway columns), which are
  taken from the events that remain;
- is kept, with the name of the check that removed it and the facts that check
  used, in a working table of the pipeline (`opdi_flight_events_rejected`).
  That table is not published.

## How it is computed

### What the aircraft was doing

For each event that a check reads, OPDI looks at the position reports of the
same track within 60 s before and after the event's time, and takes:

- the **height above the airport**: the barometric altitude of the nearest
  report that has one, minus the elevation of the airport (its height above
  sea level, from OurAirports). Barometric altitude is the altitude measured
  from air pressure, as aircraft report it, and is not corrected for the local
  pressure of the day;
- the **ground speed** of the nearest report that has one, in knots (kt);
- the **share of reports flagged on the ground** in the 120 s window.

The airport of an event is the one the event names (for example the airport of
a stand or a taxiway). An event that names none takes the departure airport of
the flight for a departure milestone (`AOBT`, `ATOT`), the destination airport
for an arrival milestone (`AIBT`, `ALDT`), and otherwise the nearer of the two
to the aircraft.

### The checks

The checks are applied in this order. An event is removed by the first check
that fires.

| Order | Check | Events read | The event is removed when |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Event without a time | every event type | it has no time. |
| 2 | Ground event while flying | `AOBT`, `AIBT`, and every entry into and exit from an area of the airport layout (`entry-{element}`, `exit-{element}`) | all three hold: the aircraft is more than 1,500 ft above the airport (more than 15,000 ft barometric altitude when the airport or its elevation is unknown); it is faster than 80 kt; and no report within 60 s is flagged on the ground. |
| 3 | Take-off or landing time too high | `ATOT`, `ALDT` | the aircraft is more than 1,500 ft above the ground at the airport (see [Height of a take-off or landing time](#height-of-a-take-off-or-landing-time)). |
| 4 | Off-block after take-off | `AOBT` | its time is at or after the take-off of the same leg. |
| 5 | In-block before landing | `AIBT` | its time is at or before the landing of the same leg. |

**Only clear evidence removes an event.** A check fires only when every fact
it needs is known and contradicts the event. When a fact is unknown, the event
is kept: for example when no report lies within 60 s of the event, when the
reports near it have no altitude, or when no take-off time was found in the
leg of an off-block time.

### Height of a take-off or landing time

A take-off or landing time is the moment the aircraft passes 15 ft above the
runway, so its height above the ground is small when it is right. Check 3
measures that height from two altitudes, both barometric:

- **The altitude at the event.** The event's own altitude, when the detector
  gave one. Otherwise the altitude is interpolated in time between the nearest
  report before the event and the nearest report after it, each within 10 s
  and each with both an altitude and a position. A jet climbs 2,000 to
  4,000 ft in a minute, so a report further away says little about the height
  at the event. When there is no such report on both sides, the height is
  unknown and the event is kept.
- **The altitude of the ground.** Barometric altitude is measured from the
  standard air pressure (1013.25 hPa). On a day of low pressure it reads too
  high, by about 27 ft per hPa: at 975 hPa, an aircraft truly 500 ft above the
  airport reads about 1,530 ft. The same error is in the altitude the aircraft
  reports while it stands or taxis at that airport. The ground level is
  therefore the aircraft's own altitude on the ground: the median altitude of
  the reports of the same track that are flagged on the ground, carry an
  altitude, and lie within 30 minutes of the event and within 5 NM of the
  airport. The difference of the two altitudes cancels the pressure error.
  When the track has no such report, which is common because reports sent on
  the ground often carry no altitude, the ground level is the airport's
  elevation and the limit is raised by 1,000 ft to cover the pressure error
  (down to about 976 hPa).

### Why these limits

- **1,500 ft above the ground.** A take-off or landing time that is close to
  the ground, though not on it, is kept. In the study of these checks, the
  airport records still confirm most take-off and landing times found between
  1,000 and 1,500 ft above the airport, and none above. The same limit is used
  for the ground events; for these, it also leaves room for the error of
  barometric altitude.
- **15,000 ft when the airport is unknown.** This is above the highest airports
  in the world, which are at about 14,500 ft.
- **80 kt.** Aircraft taxi at 10 to 30 kt. An aircraft faster than 80 kt and
  well above the airport is flying.
- **One report on the ground keeps the event.** A transponder that reports the
  aircraft on the ground within 60 s of a ground event is evidence that the
  event may be right, whatever its altitude says.
- **Order of the block times.** An aircraft cannot leave its stand after it has
  taken off, nor reach its stand before it has landed. Each block time is
  compared with the take-off or landing of its own leg: a track can hold a
  departure, an arrival and a second departure, and its first take-off says
  nothing about the off-block time of the second departure. The block time
  detector records that take-off or landing with each block time (see
  [Block times](block-times.qmd#how-it-is-computed)). A block time without
  one, for example in a track whose take-off time was not found, is not
  compared.

The other runway milestones (`line-up`, `take-off-roll`, `runway-vacated`,
the runway crossings and `xing-runway-threshold`) are not compared with the track's height:
their detector already requires the aircraft to be on or just above the
runway. Tops of climb and descent, level segments, flight-level and ring
crossings, holding, point merge, FIR crossings and go-arounds are read only
by check 1.

### Two detector rules that remove the same kind of error at the source

Two rules inside the detectors keep many implausible events from being
produced in the first place:

- **Block times from the ground part of each leg.** The off-block and in-block
  times are read only from reports that may be on the ground (flagged on the
  ground, without altitude, or at most 2,000 ft above the airport of the leg),
  and only from the part of the track on the correct side of the take-off or
  landing: the off-block time before the take-off, the in-block time after
  the landing. See [Block times](block-times.qmd#how-it-is-computed).
- **A movement from or to a standstill.** An off-block time is the start of a
  movement from a standstill: where the movement starts, the aircraft is at
  most 30 kt fast or is flagged on the ground. An in-block time is the end of
  a movement in the same way. When a track is first received while the
  aircraft is already moving fast, on the take-off roll, in the climb or on
  final approach, the moment it left the stand was not seen, and no off-block
  time is given; the same holds for an in-block time when the track ends
  while the aircraft is still moving fast.
- **Crossings over missing values.** Cleaning empties implausible altitudes,
  so a track can hold reports with no altitude in the middle of a climb. A
  crossing of a flight level, of a distance ring or of the 15 ft height that
  defines `ATOT` and `ALDT` is placed between the last report with a known
  value and the first report with a known value after the crossing. When those
  two reports are more than 30 minutes apart (60 s for the 15 ft height, which
  changes fast near the runway), no crossing is given, because its time and
  position cannot be placed. See
  [Vertical events](vertical-events.qmd#flight-level-crossings) and
  [Distance rings](distance-rings.qmd#how-it-is-computed).

## Reference data

**Airport operator records** (APDF) for 14 June 2026, from about ninety
European airports. For each movement they give the actual off-block, take-off,
landing and in-block times. They are the same kind of records as those used
for the [take-off and landing times](takeoff-landing.qmd#reference-data).

The day was computed worldwide; the records cover only the European airports
that send them.

## Validation method

The day of 14 June 2026 was computed twice from the same position reports:
once with the default settings, and once with the checks and the two detector
rules above turned off. Each `AOBT`, `ATOT`, `ALDT` and `AIBT` event of both
runs was matched to the airport record of the same flight (same aircraft
address, call sign and day) and the same milestone.

- An event is **confirmed** when it is within 60 s of the record.
- For each removed event that has a record, the study notes whether it is
  within 60 s of the record (a removed event that was right) or more than
  300 s from it (a removed event that was clearly wrong).
- For each milestone and each run, the study counts the share of the day's
  records that have an OPDI time (coverage), the share of OPDI times with a
  record that are within 60 s and 300 s of it, and the 90th percentile of the
  absolute difference.

The limits were chosen before this comparison, on the same day, from a list
of candidate checks and limits. A check was adopted only if it removed at most
0.1% of the confirmed events. The candidates that were not adopted are listed
in the [full study](../../papers/milestone-plausibility-v1/index.html).

## Results

The day, 2026-06-14, holds 6,775,827 events with the checks and the two
detector settings off. With the default settings, the checks removed 312
events:

| Check | Events removed | Of which with a record |
|---|---:|---:|
| Ground event while flying | 121 | 3 |
| Take-off or landing time too high | 0 | 0 |
| Off-block after take-off | 12 | 5 |
| In-block before landing | 179 | 76 |

By event type, they removed 12 `AOBT`, 186 `AIBT`, 38 `entry-apron`,
44 `exit-apron`, 16 `entry-taxiway` and 16 `exit-taxiway`. Most implausible
block times are no longer produced at all, because the detector reads them
only from a movement on the ground that starts or ends at a standstill (see
[Two detector rules](#two-detector-rules-that-remove-the-same-kind-of-error-at-the-source)).

Of the 84 removed events that have a record, 47 (56.0%) are more than 300 s
from it. None is within 60 s of it: the checks removed **0** of the 33,854
confirmed events.

**Block times placed in flight.** Among the block times with a known height
and speed, those more than 500 ft above the airport and faster than 80 kt:

| | `AOBT` | `AIBT` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Checks and the two detector settings off | 4,470 of 9,711 (46.03%) | 2,934 of 14,860 (19.74%) |
| Default detector, before the checks | 31 of 777 (3.99%) | 163 of 7,754 (2.10%) |
| Default settings | 27 of 765 (3.53%) | 106 of 7,568 (1.40%) |

Compared with the airport records, with the checks and the two detector
settings off and with the default settings:

| | `AOBT` off | `AOBT` default | `AIBT` off | `AIBT` default |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Records of the day | 19,349 | 19,349 | 19,514 | 19,514 |
| Coverage | 47.92% | 32.50% | 46.96% | 36.75% |
| Within 60 s | 23.00% | 34.37% | 23.07% | 31.48% |
| Within 300 s | 41.09% | 61.01% | 65.70% | 80.59% |
| 90th percentile of the absolute difference | 1,159 s | 614 s | 721 s | 407 s |
| Confirmed events | 2,167 | 2,172 | 2,204 | 2,319 |

| | `ATOT` off | `ATOT` default | `ALDT` off | `ALDT` default |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Records of the day | 19,342 | 19,342 | 19,520 | 19,520 |
| Coverage | 77.60% | 77.82% | 83.76% | 83.78% |
| Within 60 s | 90.78% | 90.72% | 94.00% | 94.00% |
| 90th percentile of the absolute difference | 59 s | 59 s | 49 s | 49 s |
| Confirmed events | 13,737 | 13,768 | 15,746 | 15,750 |

Fewer block times are published with the default settings, because wrong ones
are no longer produced or are left out, and those that remain are closer to
the records. The number of confirmed events did not fall for any of the four
milestones. Of the 2,167 confirmed off-block times of the first run, 2,163
are published at the same time with the default settings. The other four
were not at the start of a movement from a standstill: three were placed at
the first report of a track already in flight, and one during the take-off
roll; each matched its record by chance. Of the 2,204
confirmed in-block times, 2,202 are published at the same time. Of the other
two, one is published 5 s earlier and still within 60 s of its record; the
other was placed at the last report of a track still in flight, hundreds of
kilometres from its airport.

The crossing rule over missing values gave a time to 101,898 crossings that
have none when they are read from a report without a value. It gave no
crossing in 7,471 cases, where the known values are too far apart. Read from
such reports, 30,164 crossings of a flight level or a ring carry the time of
another crossing; with the rule, none does.

## Error distribution

![Height above the airport of the off-block (`AOBT`, dark) and in-block (`AIBT`, light) times of the study day, with the checks and the two detector settings off: all events, those confirmed by an airport record (within 60 s), and those more than 300 s from the record. Bar: 25th to 75th percentile; line: 5th to 95th percentile; tick: median. The dashed line is the 1,500 ft limit of the checks. Only events with a report with an altitude within 60 s are shown.](../../assets/validation/plausibility-checks_height.svg){#fig-height}

![Off-block and in-block times compared with the airport records of 2026-06-14, with the checks and the two detector settings off (light) and with the default settings (dark): share of the day's records with an OPDI time, and share of the OPDI times within 60 s and within 300 s of the record.](../../assets/validation/plausibility-checks_before_after.svg){#fig-before-after}

@fig-height shows why the height limit removes no confirmed time. The
confirmed block times lie close to the airport's elevation: 95% of the
confirmed off-block times with a known height are less than 26 ft above it,
and 95% of the confirmed in-block times less than 152 ft. The block times far
from their record spread up to several thousand feet. Most confirmed block
times have no known height at all (292 of 2,167 off-block times and 228 of
2,204 in-block times have one), because reports sent on the ground usually
carry no altitude. Such events are never removed by the height checks.

@fig-before-after shows the trade: the coverage of the block times falls, and
their agreement with the records rises.

## Headline accuracy

Confirmed milestones removed by the checks: **0** of 33,854 off-block,
in-block, take-off and landing times that are within 60 s of an airport
record, on 2026-06-14.

## Limitations

- The limits rest on one day and on the records of about ninety European
  airports. Elsewhere in the world, and on other days, the share of right
  events that are removed has not been measured.
- The checks only remove events. They do not move a wrong time to the right
  one, and they do not find an event that the detector missed. The coverage of
  the block times is therefore lower with the checks.
- An event that the track does not contradict is kept, even when it is wrong.
  A block time that is a few minutes off, or an off-block time at the wrong
  stand, passes every check.
- An `xing-runway-threshold` event (the passage over the runway threshold) is not compared
  with the track's height. Some are found more than 500 ft above the airport
  and are kept as they are.
- Tops of climb and descent, level segments, crossings, holding, point merge,
  FIR crossings and go-arounds have no check other than the missing time.
- The airport surface events accept reports up to 2,000 ft above the airport
  (see [Airport surface events](surface-events.qmd#how-it-is-computed)). Check
  2 removes such an event only when the aircraft is more than 1,500 ft above
  the airport and faster than 80 kt. An aircraft passing low or slowly over
  an airport area can still produce an entry or an exit.
- A block time still needs the track to pass a stand somewhere. When that
  passage lies in another part of the track, the time is kept but names no
  stand (see [Block times](block-times.qmd#limitations)).
- The height of the ground events uses barometric altitude without
  correction for the local air pressure, and the elevation of the airport
  from OurAirports. An error in either moves the height. For a take-off or
  landing time the pressure error is cancelled only when the track has
  reports on the ground with an altitude; otherwise an allowance of 1,000 ft
  covers pressures down to about 976 hPa, and a time at a lower pressure, or
  at an airport whose elevation is wrong by more than that, can still be
  removed.
- The removed events are not published, so a user cannot see them.
